Messages.Author: William S. Westermann

You might also want to limit unique cards to one per deck. This eliminates
lots of problems with decks consisting of alot of Catiff or weapons.
(... O.K. Igo burns and I turn over,... surprise ! Another Igo.)

Messages.Author: Alec Habig
Messages.Body:
Greg Faulkner <gsf5...@uxa.cso.uiuc.edu> wrote:
>I was considering running a tournament in my hometown, however, I dont have
>any guidelines. I've already decided on this:
>

>4 card limit

A very bad idea, unless you want the only decks that win to be Malkavian sneaky
bleed decks. See elsewhere in this newsgroup for extended discussions on why,
or email me if these have all expired. Go with no card limits. Jyhad does not
need them, and applying any card limit (especially the MtG inspired 4 card
limit) breaks the game badly (in favor of Malks).

>no Monocles

Good idea :)

>Fame is not cumulative

It's been ruled that Fame is Unique, which fixes this.

>If anyone has any other advice or a list of guidelines, please post them.

A couple days ago, Scott Johnson (sjoh...@math.scarolina.edu) posted a series
of three posts. One of them was a collated list of the offical
errata/rulings. One was a rules reference, very handy for a referee to be
familar with. The other was a set of suggested fixes/house rules this
newsgroup has come up with. For running a tourny, though, I'd be very
conservative with applying any rules that are not offical, unless you want to
piss off your players.

Also, someone recently posted what looked like a good tourny scheme - tables of
5 players, play for 2 hours, give people points for outsting their prey, and
for being alive after two hours (I forget the point values). Then mix up the
tables, and do it again (repeat several times). Group the top five point
getters into a final round, and play a standard game (no time limit, victory
points for ousting prey) to find the Champion.

Alec

This is another problem. Elimination tourneys suck. With your plan, you've
just told 1/2 your contestants "thanks for your 1/2 hour, now go away". That's
not much fun at all! Round robin style things lets everyone do what they came
to your tournament to do - play Jyhad.

Personally, I think two player Jyhad is about as much fun as two player
Diplomacy. I'd rather play MtG if there's just two players - MtG was designed
for 2 players. Jyhad was designed for multi-players. The major disadvantage
of a multi player game is that it can be hard to gather multiple players
together to play the game. A tourny totally eliminates this problem - why not
take advantage of the opprotunity to play Jyhad as it was designed??

>Also, you can do it without caring how many people want to play. The number
>of rounds can be pretty much the same,... so same amount of time.

The same with the round-robin tourny format that was mentioned earlier, only
more so.

You group people into tables of 5. These tables play for two hours. Then you
mix up the tables, and do it again.

This is an _exact_ schedule - play as many two hour rounds as your schedule
allows! Doesn't matter how many people show up, as long as there are enough
tables for them (and some tables might be short a player or two due to odd
numbers).

Give people a point for each Victory Point they get in these two hour games,
and a half point for surviving till the two hour mark.

Group the top five point getters after several rounds in a final match where
the person who ousts the most other players wins, with no time limit on the
championship round.

Playing with standardized table sizes is important for Jyhad in another way -
the deck construction rules say that the max size of a deck varies with number
of players. Unlike Magic, making a minimum sized deck is not the optimal
strategy for Jyhad. Playing with a standard table size (5 players, max 90
cards) eliminates the need for between-rounds deck reconstruction.

Actually I can think of two reasons that card limits wouldn't hurt this
deck. First, card limits would restrict intercept cards and other vote
defence cards making it more likely that your votes would pass. Second,
you can quite easily substitute other vote cards to the point where your
deck falls within a card limit scheme without weakening it much at all.
There are plenty of useful vote cards besides KRC, CA, and PS. If you
fall short at the end, just insert garbage vote cards that are just used
to push votes.

If "vote pushing" was not allowed this deck would still be possible, but
it would be as easy to shut down as any other deck.

CARD LIMITS ARE NOT THE ANSWER!!

---------
Paul Schaaf
sch...@u.washington.edu

I don't think Curt was so much pointing out your imagined cluelessness
as he was pointing out the Design Teams gross inability to correctly
interpret the rulebook in the way that the rules were intended to be used.

The official position is that KRC decks should win (actually, that's a
paraphrase - the official position is that Political Action cards can be
used to push a vote)

Obviously, this is a BadThing.

Curt (and others) sees the rules as denying the acting Methuselah the option
of playing more PAs for votes (pushing the vote).

Alan Kwan (and others) sees the rules as denying the option of playing
more than one PA by any one Methuselah to push a vote.

Both of these options can easily be read from the rules, and both are
effective ways to limit the utility of a KRC deck without detracting from
other, legitimate strategies.

Personally, I like the balanced nature of Alan Kwan's reading (no more
than one PA-card-derived vote from per Methuselah), but that's simply a
style choice.

Messages.Author: CurtAdams
Messages.Body:
bamb...@pomona.edu (Kali-Yuga) writes:

>I recently talked to a friend of mine who played in a Jyhad tourney at
Origins.
>The winning deck consisted of:
> 25 Kine Resources Contested
> 25 Conservative Agitation
> 20 Praxis Seizures

At Manafest (SF, July 1st) the winner in the second round was running a
relative of this deck. In the first round nobody had tried.

>Argue all you want about how effective a deck like this is, but I think
it
>makes a very good case for why card limits would be a good thing.
>Around here, no one has more than 5 of any card, so card limits never
become
>an issue, though, which is nice.

This has come up before, and the discussions have been long and involved
enough that the above type of deck has a name - the "KRC" deck. I'm going
to reiterate my previous arguments, with some changes and reorganizations.
I apologize to those who have seen this before, but it is the nature of
netgroups to rehash subjects since membership changes so constantly.

There are three problems with fixing this deck with card limits:

1) A successful fix of this problem carries a horrible price.
2) Any fix of this problem via card limits is inherently temporary.
3) The rules already are written to handle the problem this deck is an
example of (and the problem is much more fundamental than KRC decks)
Admittedly, our friends at the design team insist we should ignore the
rulebooks (both of them) on this one, although I'm completely at a loss
for a reason for that.

As a bit of background, the KRC deck is only an implementation of a very
fundamental problem, the "all vote" deck. Consider the following
generalization of the above deck:

2 of each Praxis Seizure
50 Votes.
A couple of cards to get out more vampires - Effective Management, 3rd
Tradition, etc.
Lots of weenies in the crypt.

Now by the DT rules, this deck will frequently pop out a swarm of
vampires, title most of them, and then proceed to call an absolute
blizzard of votes. It can basically get 5-8 votes for any referendum
called via pitching cards from its hand (which is obviously mostly votes),
plus any votes from previous title seizures. It can pretty much pass any
vote in the deck for as many times as the vote is present.

There's too many vampires to rush, too many votes called to intercept, and
too many votes for to Debate (Surprise Influence/Dread Gaze/etc.) Only
decks with large numbers of specialty cards have a good chance against
this (Delaying Tactics and Justine).

Essentially you have a vote deck which can bypass most of the standard
anti-vote strategies. At the same time, unlike every other kind of Jyhad
decks, which must assemble combinations to take actions, it can use
political actions to both call and pass votes. The deck avoids the two of
the critical controls on Jyhad decks - general purpose counterstrategies
and the need for combinations. That's lethal

Now the way card limits "fix" this problem is by restricting the number of
useful aggressive votes. With only 5 KRC and 5 CA, damage to prey in a 5
player game is limited to 35 pool, less intercepted votes and less the
deterioration of CA as the number of players drops. More typically, many
of the aggressive votes get intercepted, and the actual maximum is far
less than that. It can't win.

But the same limits apply to EVERY vote deck! Actually, they are much
worse for other vote decks. The other (healthy) vote decks must still
deal with the usual need to assemble combinations in their hands
(political actions plus votes to pass them) and must deal with all the
traditional anti-vote strategies (intercept, rush, and debate). To stop
the KRC deck, you've stopped ALL vote strategies. Jyhad stands on a
tripod of strategies (bleed, combat, and vote), and you've just kicked out
one of the legs. That's the horrible price you pay.

Now the exact # of cards that turns off a KRC deck isn't clear. You can
actually do a little more than just KRC and CA - Sabbat Threat, 1st
Tradition, and Anarch Revolt fit in nicely - but no matter what your
limit, the all-vote decks trump all other vote decks. If an all-vote deck
doesn't do great, no other vote deck even does well.

Further card limits haven't fixed the real problem, just papered it over
(really all they ever do). If we ever get any expansions for Jyhad, you
can be sure there will be more votes to hurt prey, one way or another.
Once you have enough anti-prey votes, all-vote KRC decks will romp forth
in all their foul glory - and the fact that the pictures on their cards
show a little more variety won't amount to a hill of beans.

Now this problem with all-vote decks is a pretty nasty one. Garfield is
an excellent game designer, and WotC's playtesting resources were pretty
extensive by the time they made Jyhad. Would they really have left a hole
so big you could drive a truck through? (i.e., win at Origins) I think
not.

Check the rulebook (either one) and it says that any OTHER methuseleh can
throw in political action cards for votes. The caller can only use the
vote from the card he used to call the referendum. There's no provision
that allows the Meth calling the vote to throw any additional political
action cards. This is a mighty peculiar rule - until you realize that it
shuts down all-vote decks (KRC or otherwise) while not appreciably
restricting normal, healthy, vote decks.

The earlier (playtest) rule had been that political action cards did NOT
provide any votes (Garfield, The Eternal Struggle). If you switch to the
rulebook rules, healthy vote decks aren't much affected - they gain one
vote, and most opponents will not be running vote decks and hence have no
PA cards to throw. They still have titles, Bewitching Orations, Bribes,
Scorn of Adonis, Telepathic Vote Counting, and Charming Lobby.

If the rules weren't so clear (and so odd), I'd write this off to a
mistake. Jyhad is a well-balanced CCG and they obviously caught most of
the problems, but they did miss a few things - the untap cards, and a few
others. But claiming the missed a major (and simple) game problem AND
accidentally miswrote the rules in such a way as to fix it strains
credulity.
Curt Adams (curt...@aol.com)

Messages.Body:
lsc...@crl.com (L. Scott Johnson) writes:

>In article <3ugnbl$9...@tierra.santafe.edu>, Bret Ambrose <ambrose>
wrote:
>>curt...@aol.com (CurtAdams) wrote:

>>>Check the rulebook (either one) and it says that any OTHER methuseleh
can
>>>throw in political action cards for votes. The caller can only use the
>>>vote from the card he used to call the referendum. There's no
provision
>>>that allows the Meth calling the vote to throw any additional political
>>>action cards. This is a mighty peculiar rule - until you realize that
it
>>>shuts down all-vote decks (KRC or otherwise) while not appreciably
>>>restricting normal, healthy, vote decks.
>

>>Hmm, you're right, maybe I should get a clue before posting about such
>>things. Then again, nobody else I play with has noticed it either.
>>If this is the case, then why are KRC decks winning, though? I suppose
>>if you get enough titles out in the early game, you'll be ok.
>>Thanks for pointing this out, though.

>I don't think Curt was so much pointing out your imagined cluelessness
>as he was pointing out the Design Teams gross inability to correctly
>interpret the rulebook in the way that the rules were intended to be
used.

Bingo. There's no "cluenessness" involved here. The rule is a very
counterintuitive rule that serves a good purpose.

>The official position is that KRC decks should win (actually, that's a
>paraphrase - the official position is that Political Action cards can be
>used to push a vote)

>Obviously, this is a BadThing.

>Curt (and others) sees the rules as denying the acting Methuselah the
option
>of playing more PAs for votes (pushing the vote).

>Alan Kwan (and others) sees the rules as denying the option of playing
>more than one PA by any one Methuselah to push a vote.

>Both of these options can easily be read from the rules, and both are
>effective ways to limit the utility of a KRC deck without detracting from
>other, legitimate strategies.

>Personally, I like the balanced nature of Alan Kwan's reading (no more
>than one PA-card-derived vote from per Methuselah), but that's simply a
>style choice.

I also agree that Alan's suggestion would make for more interesting games;
I just can't see his reading of the rules. Unfortunately, he hasn't got
net access during the summer to defend his suggestion.

The standard reading of the rules (Bret's earlier reading) IS very
natural. When I first read the rulebook, I saw that the rules prohibited
pushing your own vote - and promptly dismissed that as "ridiculous".
*Obviously* the rules were in error. Only when the weenie vote got
discussed a while back did I realize what an excellent rule prohibited
pushing your own votes was.

Curt Adams (curt...@aol.com)
